text: raw_customers is sitting in Snowflake, and dbt is connected to that database — but dbt doesn't actually know the table exists yet, not until it's declared as a source. That's this lesson, written for real against this project's own data.

Here's the real file: models, staging, jaffle_shop, src underscore jaffle_shop dot yml. Version 2, a sources block, name jaffle_shop, database jaffle_shop_raw, schema public, and under tables, name raw_customers. Compare this to the prerequisite dbt course's own example — same shape, same keys, just pointed at this project's real database from Lesson 3 and this project's real table.

Once declared, the staging model you'll write next lesson references it like this: select star from source, jaffle_shop, raw_customers. Two arguments — the source name, then the table name — not a hardcoded jaffle_shop_raw dot public dot raw_customers string. That function call resolves to the real table at run time.

You could skip source() and just hardcode the table path — it would even work, for a project this size. But declaring it properly buys you three real things. It shows up in the lineage graph as a real starting node. It becomes testable — Lesson 7's not_null and unique tests can point at a source column exactly like a model column. And freshness checks become available for free, the moment it's declared.

Here's the practical payoff. If this table ever moved to a different schema, and every model had hardcoded its path, every one of those models would break. With source(), exactly one line in sources.yml changes, and every model using source('jaffle_shop', 'raw_customers') keeps working without a single edit.

With a real, working sources.yml in place, the raw data is now known to dbt, not just sitting in Snowflake. Next lesson, we build the staging model itself — stg_jaffle_shop__customers.sql, using this exact source() call.
